mainTopic: Pesachim 21b: The ban on benefit from חמץ, and whether every Torah eating ban also forbids benefit
overview: This amud opens with the end of a ברייתא: רבי יהודה בן בתירא forbids selling כותח to a non-Jew for thirty days before פסח. The גמרא then goes through three clauses of the משנה. For each one it asks 'פשיטא, isn't that obvious?' and answers 'לא צריכא, it is needed for a special case.' The three cases are: חמץ charred before its time stays permitted (like רבא); benefit is forbidden even in the rabbinic hours (proved from רבי יוחנן's ruling on קידושין); and even according to רבי יהודה, who requires burning, one may not use the fire of burning חמץ. Next, חזקיה learns the ban on benefit from the passive wording 'לא יאכל חמץ'. This implies that a plain eating ban would not forbid benefit, which disagrees with רבי אבהו. רבי אבהו says every eating ban includes benefit unless the Torah allows it, as it did with נבילה. The גמרא then brings the ברייתא on נבילה, where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue over giving and selling it to a גר or a גוי, and explains how each one reads the word 'או'. Finally, the גמרא shows that רבי אבהו's rule fits both views. רבי מאיר learns it from the נבילה verse, and רבי יהודה learns it from 'לַכֶּלֶב תַּשְׁלִיכוּן אֹתוֹ', which the גמרא continues to explain on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי יהודה בן בתירא on selling כותח
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בתירא rules that כותח and anything like it may not be sold to a non-Jew in the thirty days before פסח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בתירא says: כותח and all kinds of כותח may not be sold during the thirty days before פסח.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of a ברייתא about selling חמץ to a non-Jew before פסח. רבי יהודה בן בתירא adds a special rule for כותח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כותח is a sharp dip made with bread crumbs, so people use only a little at a time. A non-Jew who buys it now will probably still have it on פסח, so a Jew should not sell it to him for a full thirty days beforehand.

keyTerms.meaning: A sharp dip made with leavened bread crumbs

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:
Kutach and all types of kutach,
phrases.notes: A dip containing leavened bread crumbs

phrases.aramaic: אָסוּר לִמְכּוֹר שְׁלֹשִׁים יוֹם קוֹדֶם לַפֶּסַח.
phrases.english: it is forbidden to sell [it] thirty days before Pesach.
phrases.notes: It is used slowly, so it will last until Pesach

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the ברייתא from the previous amud (21a) about selling חמץ to a non-Jew before פסח
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כותח may not be sold to a non-Jew for thirty days before פסח because it lasts a long time.

steps.title: Why say חמץ is permitted for benefit before its time?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line 'it is permitted for benefit' and asks why that needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה said:] 'And it is permitted for benefit.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns back to the משנה. It quotes the clause saying that חמץ may be used for benefit while it may still be eaten, and asks why the משנה bothered to say it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you are allowed to eat the חמץ at that time, you are surely allowed to benefit from it in other ways. So the clause looks unnecessary, and the גמרא wants to find what new point it teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Permitted to benefit from (not only eating)
It is obvious! (why does it need to be said?)

steps.confusionAlert: 'פשיטא' does not mean the גמרא thinks the משנה is wrong. It is asking what new thing the משנה is teaching, since every word of a משנה should teach something.

phrases.english: [The mishna said:] 'And it is permitted for benefit.'
That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: going through the clauses of the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whatever may be eaten may obviously be used for benefit, so the clause seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Needed for חמץ charred before its time
steps.stepSummary: The clause is needed for חמץ that was burned until inedible before the deadline. It teaches the same rule that רבא states.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where he charred it before its time. And it teaches us like רבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the clause is about a special case: חמץ that was charred before it became forbidden. This sets up the quote from רבא in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's word 'permitted' is not about ordinary bread. It covers bread that was charred while still permitted, and teaches that this bread stays permitted for benefit. That is exactly the view of רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (for a specific case)
He charred it (burned it until it cannot be eaten)
Before its time (before חמץ becomes forbidden)

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where he charred it before its time.
And it teaches us in accordance with Rava,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the clause to a specific case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clause seemed to be about ordinary חמץ before its time, which is obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause is about חמץ charred before its time, which stays permitted for benefit.

steps.title: רבא: charred חמץ stays permitted
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that חמץ charred before its time may be used for benefit even after the time of the איסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבא said: if he charred it before its time, it is permitted for benefit even after its time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבא's ruling, which is the rule the משנה is teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the bread is charred and cannot be eaten before the איסור starts, it is no longer considered food or חמץ. So when the deadline comes there is nothing to forbid, and the benefit stays permitted afterward too.

keyTerms.meaning: After its time (once חמץ is forbidden)
אמורא whose ruling the משנה is shown to teach

steps.whatToRemember: חמץ that was charred until inedible before the deadline stops being חמץ and stays permitted for benefit even on פסח (רבא).

phrases.english: As Rava said:
[If] he charred it before its time,
it is permitted for benefit even after its time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the ruling of רבא that step 3 said the משנה teaches
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חמץ charred before its time is permitted for benefit even after its time.

steps.title: Why say חמץ is forbidden after its time?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next clause, 'once its time passes it is forbidden for benefit', and asks why it needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה said:] 'Once its time has passed, it is forbidden for benefit.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next clause of the משנה and asks the same question again: isn't this obvious?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone knows that חמץ on פסח is forbidden for benefit. So stating that it becomes forbidden after its time seems to add nothing.

phrases.english: [The mishna said:] 'Once its time passes, it is forbidden for benefit.'
That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as step 2, applied to the next clause
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's clause 'עבר זמנו אסור בהנאתו'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It is well known that חמץ is forbidden for benefit, so the clause seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Needed for the rabbinic hours
steps.stepSummary: The clause teaches that even during the extra hours forbidden only by the חכמים, benefit from חמץ is already forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for the hours that are forbidden by rabbinic law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the clause is about the hours on ערב פסח when חמץ is forbidden only מדרבנן (starting at the sixth hour). The next step brings support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה forbids חמץ from midday. The חכמים added an earlier hour as a safeguard. The משנה is teaching that during this rabbinic time, benefit is also fully forbidden, not just eating.

keyTerms.meaning: The hours forbidden by rabbinic decree (before midday on ערב פסח)

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
for the hours [forbidden] by rabbinic law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the clause to a specific case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clause seemed to be about the Torah-level איסור, which is obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause teaches that benefit is forbidden even during the rabbinic hours.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: קידושין with חמץ in the sixth hour are void
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that someone who betroths a woman with חמץ from the sixth hour onward has no valid קידושין, even with very hard wheat.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב גידל said in the name of רב חייא בר יוסף in the name of רבי יוחנן: one who betroths from six hours and on, even with hard mountain wheat, we do not worry that the betrothal took effect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's ruling to show that the rabbinic איסור הנאה in those hours has real force.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קידושין needs an object worth at least a פרוטה. Something forbidden for benefit is worth nothing. Since the קידושין fail even in the rabbinic hours, and even with hard wheat that might not have become חמץ at all, the rabbinic איסור הנאה clearly applies in full.

keyTerms.meaning: Hard mountain wheat, unlikely to become leavened
We are not concerned that the betrothal is valid

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a rabbinic איסור הנאה can make an object legally worthless, strong enough to cancel קידושין.
steps.whatToRemember: From the sixth hour on ערב פסח, חמץ is already forbidden for benefit מדרבנן. It counts as worthless, so קידושין made with it do not take effect.

phrases.english: As Rav Giddel said
[that] Rav Chiya bar Yosef said
[that] Rabbi Yochanan said:
One who betroths [with chametz] from six hours and onward,
even with hard mountain wheat,
phrases.notes: Wheat so hard it probably did not become leavened

phrases.english: we are not concerned for the betrothal.
phrases.notes: Something forbidden for benefit has no value

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב גִּידֵּל אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 6's claim that the rabbinic hours carry a full איסור הנאה
steps.raayaObject: That חמץ is forbidden for benefit during the rabbinic hours
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's ruling that קידושין with חמץ from the sixth hour are void

steps.title: Why say not to fuel an oven with חמץ?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the clause 'one may not light an oven or stove with it' and asks why it is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה said:] 'And one may not light an oven or stove with it.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the third clause and asks again: isn't this obvious?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Using חמץ as fuel to heat an oven is plainly a kind of benefit. The משנה already said benefit is forbidden, so this line seems to repeat itself.

phrases.english: [The mishna said:] 'And one may not light an oven or stove with it.'
That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern, applied to the third clause
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's clause 'ולא יסיק בו תנור וכירים'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fueling an oven is benefit, and benefit was already forbidden, so the clause seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Needed according to רבי יהודה's view that חמץ must be burned
steps.stepSummary: The clause is needed according to רבי יהודה, who holds that חמץ may be destroyed only by burning.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed according to רבי יהודה, who said that removing חמץ is only by burning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the clause matters according to רבי יהודה. The next step explains what mistake we might have made without it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יהודה, burning is the required way to get rid of חמץ. Because the מצוה itself involves fire, there is room to think the fire could also be put to use.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
according to Rabbi Yehuda, who said
the removal of chametz is only by burning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the clause is needed according to a specific opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fueling an oven is simply benefit, which is obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause is needed to teach רבי יהודה's followers that benefit is forbidden even during the burning.

steps.title: No benefit even while burning it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the mistaken assumption: since the מצוה is burning, one might think he may benefit from the fire. The משנה teaches that he may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought: since רבי יהודה said its מצוה is by burning, while he burns it let him benefit from it. So it teaches us [that he may not].
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer by spelling out the mistake the משנה prevents: thinking that while you burn חמץ for the מצוה, you may cook or heat with that fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though burning is the מצוה, the איסור הנאה does not go away while the חמץ burns. The חמץ must be burned without using its fire, so the clause about the oven and stove is not repetitive.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have thought to say

steps.whatToRemember: Each of the three clauses has a new point: (1) charred חמץ stays permitted (רבא); (2) benefit is forbidden even in the rabbinic hours; (3) even according to רבי יהודה, one may not benefit from the fire while burning חמץ.

phrases.english: It could have entered your mind to say:

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וְאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה מִצְוָתוֹ בִּשְׂרֵיפָה,
phrases.english: since Rabbi Yehuda said its מצוה is by burning,
while he is burning it
let him benefit from it;
[therefore] it teaches us [that he may not].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes step 9 by stating the הוה אמינא and the lesson
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even when burning is the מצוה of ביעור, it is forbidden to benefit from the fire of burning חמץ.

steps.title: חזקיה's source that benefit from חמץ is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה derives the ban on benefit from חמץ from the wording 'לא יאכל חמץ': there should be no permitted 'eating' of it at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said: Where do we learn that benefit from חמץ on פסח is forbidden? The verse says 'חמץ shall not be eaten.' This means there should be nothing about it that is allowed to be 'eaten', not even through benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement begins. חזקיה gives a verse showing that חמץ on פסח is forbidden not only to eat but also to use for any benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse uses a passive form, 'it shall not be eaten,' instead of 'you shall not eat.' חזקיה reads this as saying the חמץ itself must have no permitted 'eating' at all. That includes benefit, since you could sell it and use the money to buy food.

keyTerms.meaning: a ban on getting any benefit or use from an item
'it shall not be eaten' (the passive form)
any permitted way of 'eating', meaning any allowed use

phrases.english: Chizkiya said:
From where do we know that leavened bread on Pesach
is forbidden for benefit?
As it says: 'Leavened bread shall not be eaten'.
phrases.notes: The passive form is the key to the derivation.

phrases.english: There shall be no permitted 'eating' of it at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר חִזְקִיָּה: מִנַּיִן לְחָמֵץ בַּפֶּסַח שֶׁאָסוּר בַּהֲנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the Torah source for the benefit ban that the earlier steps assumed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The benefit ban on חמץ comes from the passive wording 'לא יאכל'.

steps.title: Inference: without this wording, only eating would be forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from חזקיה that a plain eating ban would not, by itself, imply a benefit ban.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is that the Torah wrote 'חמץ shall not be eaten.' If it had not written 'shall not be eaten,' I would have said that only eating is forbidden, and benefit is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from חזקיה's words. It shows what his view assumes about ordinary eating bans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חזקיה needed the special passive wording to forbid benefit. That shows he holds that a normal phrase like 'you shall not eat' only forbids eating. This inference sets up the clash with רבי אבהו in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: the reason is (often introduces an inference)
I would have said (a mistaken assumption)

phrases.english: The reason is that the Merciful One wrote
'Leavened bread shall not be eaten';
but had it not written 'shall not be eaten',
I would have said:
a prohibition of eating is implied,
a prohibition of benefit is not implied.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws out what חזקיה's derivation assumes.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: For חזקיה, a plain eating ban does not include a benefit ban.

steps.title: This disagrees with רבי אבהו's general rule
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו holds that every eating ban also forbids benefit unless the Torah says otherwise, as it did with נבילה. This contradicts the inference from חזקיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with רבי אבהו. רבי אבהו said: Wherever the Torah says 'it shall not be eaten,' 'you shall not eat' (singular), or 'you shall not eat' (plural), both eating and benefit are forbidden. That holds unless the Torah spells out that benefit is allowed, as it did with נבילה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that חזקיה's view conflicts with רבי אבהו. It then quotes רבי אבהו's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי אבהו, any form of 'do not eat' already includes 'do not benefit.' So the special passive wording is not needed. The only exceptions are cases where the Torah openly allows benefit, such as נבילה.

keyTerms.meaning: an animal that died without proper שחיטה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי אבהו says benefit is allowed. He is stricter than the inference from חזקיה: every eating ban automatically includes benefit.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Rabbi Abahu.
For Rabbi Abahu said:
Wherever it is stated
'It shall not be eaten,' 'You (singular) shall not eat,' 'You (plural) shall not eat',

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד אִיסּוּר אֲכִילָה וְאֶחָד אִיסּוּר הֲנָאָה (מַשְׁמַע),
phrases.english: both a prohibition of eating and a prohibition of benefit are implied,
unless the verse spells it out for you
the way it spelled it out for you regarding a carcass.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the inference in step 12 contradicts a competing view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any Torah eating ban includes a benefit ban unless the Torah explicitly allows benefit.

steps.title: The ברייתא on נבילה: רבי מאיר allows giving or selling to anyone
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא shows that the Torah explicitly allows benefit from נבילה. רבי מאיר reads the verse as allowing it to be given or sold to both a גר תושב and a נכרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the ברייתא teaches: 'Do not eat any נבילה. Give it to the stranger in your gates so he can eat it, or sell it to a foreigner.' From this alone, I would only know giving to a גר and selling to a נכרי. How do we know selling to a גר? The verse says 'to the stranger in your gates you may give it, or sell.' How do we know giving to a נכרי? The verse says 'you may give it so he may eat it, or sell it to a foreigner.' So we conclude: both a גר and a נכרי may receive it, whether by sale or as a gift. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא that רבי אבהו relied on. The Torah had to spell out that benefit from נבילה is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the Torah had to say openly that נבילה may be given or sold, we see that without this, 'do not eat' would have forbidden benefit too. That supports רבי אבהו. רבי מאיר reads the verse's parts together, so giving and selling each apply to both the גר and the נכרי.

keyTerms.meaning: as was taught in a ברייתא
a non-Jew living in the Land who accepted the seven Noahide laws

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:
'You shall not eat any carcass;
to the stranger who is in your gates you shall give it, that he may eat it,
or sell it to a foreigner, etc.'
I have only giving to a resident alien
and selling to a gentile.
From where do we know selling to a resident alien?
The verse teaches:
'To the stranger in your gates you shall give it, or sell.'
From where do we know giving to a gentile?
The verse teaches:
'You shall give it that he may eat it, or sell it to a foreigner.'
So you end up saying:
both a resident alien and a gentile,
whether by selling or by giving,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for רבי אבהו's example of נבילה.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אבהו's claim that the Torah had to explicitly allow benefit from נבילה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on 'לא תאכלו כל נבלה' (דברים יד:כא)

steps.title: רבי יהודה: the verse means exactly what it says
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rules that the verse is literal: give to a גר, and sell to a נכרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: The words mean just what they say. Giving is for a גר, and selling is for a נכרי.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא presents רבי יהודה's opposing view. He reads the verse literally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה does not mix the methods between the two recipients. A גר gets the נבילה as a gift, and a נכרי gets it only by sale. Both agree that benefit from נבילה is allowed. They argue only about how it may be passed on.

keyTerms.meaning: the words are as written (read literally)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says,
the words are as they are written:
to a resident alien by giving
and to a gentile by selling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposing view within the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נבילה may be given only to a גר and sold only to a נכרי.

steps.title: What is רבי יהודה's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what in the verse leads רבי יהודה to read it literally.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רבי יהודה's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of רבי יהודה's view. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a challenge. The גמרא wants to know which textual detail supports the literal reading over רבי מאיר's broader one.

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the basis of רבי יהודה's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The textual basis for רבי יהודה's literal reading

steps.title: The word 'או' shows the verse is literal
steps.stepSummary: If רבי מאיר were right, the Torah would have written 'and sell.' Writing 'או' (or) separates the two cases, so the words are literal.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think it is like רבי מאיר said, then the Torah should have written: 'To the stranger in your gates give it, that he may eat it, and sell.' Why do I need the word 'or'? Learn from it that the words mean exactly what they say.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה learns his view from the word 'או' in the verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Writing 'and' would have joined giving and selling into one list for both recipients. Writing 'or' splits the verse into two separate cases: giving goes with the גר, and selling goes with the נכרי. So רבי יהודה reads each method as tied to its own recipient.

keyTerms.meaning: if it entered your mind (if you were to think)

steps.whatToRemember: חזקיה needs the special wording 'לא יאכל' to forbid benefit from חמץ. רבי אבהו says every eating ban already includes benefit unless the Torah allows it, as with נבילה. Within the נבילה ברייתא, רבי מאיר lets either method go to either recipient, while רבי יהודה reads it literally because of the word 'או'.

phrases.english: If it should enter your mind
as Rabbi Meir said,
let the Merciful One write:
'To the stranger who is in your gates
you shall give it, that he may eat it, and sell.'
Why do I need 'or'?
Learn from it that the words are as they are written.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ כִּדְאָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about רבי יהודה's reason.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'או' instead of 'and' shows that giving and selling are tied to separate recipients.

steps.title: What does רבי מאיר do with the word 'or'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי מאיר explains the word 'או' in the verse, since רבי יהודה used that word to prove his literal reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי מאיר? [What does he do with the word 'or'?]
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבי מאיר and asks what he does with the word 'או' (or). This is a short setup question, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 17, רבי יהודה argued that 'או' splits the verse into two separate cases. רבי מאיר does not split it that way, so the word 'או' seems extra for him. The גמרא wants to know what extra lesson he takes from it.

keyTerms.meaning: And רבי מאיר? (a short way of asking how this תנא answers the point just made)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir? [How does he explain the word 'or'?]
phrases.notes: A two-word question. The full meaning is understood from what came before.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns רבי יהודה's proof from the word 'או' back onto רבי מאיר
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What lesson רבי מאיר learns from the word 'או'

steps.title: For רבי מאיר, 'or' teaches who comes first
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר uses 'או' to teach that giving to a גר comes before selling to a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'or' teaches that giving to a גר takes priority over selling to a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי מאיר reads 'או' as a lesson about order. Giving the נבילה to a גר comes before selling it to a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר still holds that both giving and selling are allowed to both people. For him, 'או' does not limit anything. It only ranks the options, putting the needy גר ahead of the paying גוי.

keyTerms.meaning: To put first; to give priority

phrases.english: 'Or' comes to give precedence to
phrases.notes: The word 'או' in the verse is being explained.

phrases.english: giving to a resident alien
over selling to a gentile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'או' teaches a priority: give to the גר before selling to the גוי

steps.title: Where does רבי יהודה get this priority?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי יהודה knows the priority rule, since he already used 'או' for something else.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה? [Where does he learn that the גר comes first?]
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא turns to רבי יהודה. He used up the word 'או' for his literal reading, so where does he learn that the גר comes first? This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each side has to account for the same verse. If רבי מאיר needs 'או' to teach the priority, it looks as if רבי יהודה has no source for that priority.

keyTerms.meaning: And רבי יהודה? (how does this תנא handle the point?)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda? [From where does he learn this priority?]

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns רבי מאיר's lesson about priority onto רבי יהודה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What רבי יהודה's source is for putting the גר before the גוי

steps.title: For רבי יהודה, the priority is simple logic
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה needs no verse for the priority. We are commanded to support a גר and not a גוי, so the גר obviously comes first.
steps.simpleTranslation: This does not need a verse. You are commanded to keep a גר alive, and you are not commanded to keep a גוי alive. So no verse is needed; it is logic.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה does not need a verse to know the גר comes first. Plain logic already tells us this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a מצוה to support a גר תושב, but no such duty toward a גוי. So it makes sense that the גר gets priority. Since logic teaches the priority, the word 'או' is free for רבי יהודה to use for his literal reading.

keyTerms.meaning: To keep him alive; to support him

phrases.english: This does not need a verse:
since a resident alien,
you are commanded to sustain him,
phrases.notes: Based on the verse in ויקרא 25:35 about supporting a גר תושב.

phrases.english: and a gentile, you are not
commanded to sustain him,
there is no need for a verse; it is logic.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 and closes the discussion of the word 'או'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The priority comes from logic, because there is a duty to support a גר and no such duty toward a גוי
steps.whatToRemember: Both תנאים agree the גר comes first. רבי מאיר learns it from 'או'. רבי יהודה learns it from logic, which leaves 'או' free for his literal reading.

steps.title: For רבי מאיר, רבי אבהו's rule works
steps.stepSummary: For רבי מאיר, the verse allows full benefit from נבילה. Since the Torah needed a verse to allow it, all other eating bans must forbid benefit, just as רבי אבהו said.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense according to רבי מאיר, who said both a גר and a גוי may receive it, whether by selling or by giving. Since a verse was needed to allow benefit from נבילה, it follows that all prohibitions in the Torah forbid both eating and benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the discussion back to רבי אבהו from step 13. It shows that his rule fits רבי מאיר well, and this sets up a question on רבי יהודה in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי מאיר, the verse's job is to allow benefit from נבילה in every way. If the Torah needed to say this, then without such a verse, an eating ban would also forbid benefit. That is exactly רבי אבהו's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (opens a contrast: 'this works for one view, but...')
In benefit; using it for gain

phrases.english: It works well according to Rabbi Meir, who said:
both a resident alien and a gentile,
whether through selling or through giving.
Since a verse was needed
to permit benefit from an animal carcass,
it follows that all prohibitions in the Torah
are forbidden both in eating and in benefit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side point about 'או' and returns to רבי אבהו's rule
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, the need for a verse allowing benefit from נבילה proves that eating bans normally forbid benefit
steps.confusionAlert: 'בשלמא' does not end the discussion. It means 'this view works fine', and it always leads into an 'אלא' question about the other view.

steps.title: For רבי יהודה, where does the rule come from?
steps.stepSummary: For רבי יהודה, the verse only teaches its literal rule: give to the גר, sell to the נכרי. So the source for רבי אבהו's rule seems to be missing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רבי יהודה, who said the verse comes to teach things as written, from where does he know that all prohibitions in the Torah forbid benefit?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה's view. If the verse teaches only the literal rules, it no longer proves that eating bans also forbid benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, the verse is spent on its literal details: give to the גר, sell to the גוי. So it cannot also teach that benefit needed special permission. Without that, רבי אבהו's rule has no source in his view.

keyTerms.meaning: But (the second half of a בשלמא question)
From where does he know it?

phrases.english: But according to Rabbi Yehuda, who said:
the verse comes to teach the matters as they are written,
then all prohibitions in the Torah,
from where does he know that they are forbidden in benefit?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The 'אלא' half of the בשלמא structure begun in step 22
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's view, as a basis for רבי אבהו's rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה reads the verse literally, so it no longer shows that benefit needed permission. That removes the proof for רבי אבהו's rule.

steps.title: רבי יהודה learns it from 'throw it to the dog'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה learns that eating bans forbid benefit from the verse about טריפה: 'לַכֶּלֶב תַּשְׁלִיכוּן אֹתוֹ'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from 'you shall throw it to the dog'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה has a different source. He uses the verse about טריפה, which says to throw it to the dog.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה does not need the נבילה verse for this rule. He gets it from 'לַכֶּלֶב תַּשְׁלִיכוּן אֹתוֹ' (שמות 22:30). The גמרא will go on to explain exactly how this verse teaches the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You shall throw it to the dog' (שמות 22:30, said about טריפה)
An animal with a fatal defect

phrases.english: He derives it
phrases.notes: The verse is in שמות 22:30, in the section about טריפה.

phrases.english: from 'you shall throw it to the dog.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without the נבילה verse, רבי יהודה seems to have no source for the rule
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה learns the rule from 'לַכֶּלֶב תַּשְׁלִיכוּן אֹתוֹ'
steps.whatToRemember: Both תנאים can agree with רבי אבהו's rule. רבי מאיר learns it from the נבילה verse. רבי יהודה learns it from 'לַכֶּלֶב תַּשְׁלִיכוּן אֹתוֹ'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that רבי אבהו's rule does not depend on one side of the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה.
